Text: SHA-256 produces a {{c1::256-bit}} ({{c2::32-byte}}) fixed-size digest from any input. It is computationally infeasible to reverse due to {{c3::nonlinear bit operations}} that destroy input directionality.
Extra: Collision resistance: no two inputs have been found that produce the same SHA-256 hash.

Text: `MessageDigest.getInstance("{{c1::SHA-256}}")` returns a digest engine. Calling {{c2::`.digest(bytes)`}} applies the hash and returns the raw byte array output.
Base64 is {{c1::an encoding scheme}}, NOT {{c2::encryption}}. Anyone can {{c3::decode}} a Base64 string without a key. It provides {{c4::zero confidentiality}}.
Extra: Base64 encodes binary data as 64-character ASCII text for safe transmission in text-only protocols.

Text: `java.util.Random` uses a {{c1::Linear Congruential Generator (LCG)}} algorithm that is {{c2::deterministic and predictable}} from observed outputs. Use {{c3::java.security.SecureRandom}} for all cryptographic values.
Extra: SecureRandom sources entropy from the OS kernel (/dev/urandom on Linux), making its output cryptographically unpredictable.

Text: Passwords should be stored in {{c1::char[]}} instead of {{c2::String}} because `char[]` can be explicitly {{c3::zeroed with `Arrays.fill()`}} immediately after use, while `String` is {{c4::immutable and retained in JVM heap}} until GC.
Code: char[] password = getPassword();\n// use password\nArrays.fill(password, '\0'); // immediate clear

Text: SQL injection occurs when user input {{c1::alters the structure}} of a SQL query. The fix is to use {{c2::PreparedStatement}} with {{c3::parameterized placeholders (`?`)}}, which treats user input as a {{c4::literal value, not SQL syntax}}.
Code: PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?");\nps.setString(1, userInput);

Text: Insecure deserialization is dangerous because `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` {{c1::instantiates classes from the byte stream before validation}}, enabling {{c2::gadget chains}} that invoke {{c3::Runtime.exec()}} — a form of {{c4::Remote Code Execution (RCE)}}.
Extra: ObjectInputFilter mitigates this by rejecting classes not in the whitelist before they are instantiated.

Text: `ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter("com.example.*;!*")` creates a filter that {{c1::allows only `com.example.*` classes}} and {{c2::rejects all others (`!*`)}} before {{c3::instantiation occurs}} during deserialization.

AES encryption uses {{c1::Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding")}}. A {{c2::unique random IV}} must be generated with {{c3::SecureRandom}} per encryption to prevent ciphertext repetition with the same key.
Code: byte[] iv = new byte[16]; new SecureRandom().nextBytes(iv);

Text: A cryptographic {{c1::salt}} is a {{c2::random value}} added to a password before hashing. It prevents {{c3::rainbow table}} attacks by ensuring that two users with the same password have {{c4::different stored hashes}}.
Extra: Generated with: `byte[] salt = new byte[16]; new SecureRandom().nextBytes(salt);`

Text: MD5 and SHA-1 are {{c1::broken}} for cryptographic use because {{c2::real collision attacks}} have been demonstrated. Java applications should use at minimum {{c3::SHA-256}} for integrity and hashing.
Extra: SHA-1 collision: Google's "SHAttered" attack (2017) demonstrated two PDFs with identical SHA-1 hashes.

Text: `KeyStore` is Java's {{c1::encrypted container}} for {{c2::cryptographic keys and certificates}}. It is initialized with `KeyStore.getInstance("{{c3::PKCS12}}")` and protected by a {{c4::password}}.
